newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian jobs market gaining strength in 97.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian jobs market gaining strength in 97.

text.p: Economists on Thursday detected a heartbeat in the Australian labour market which may be sufficient to rule out another official interest rate cut, but the jobs growth has yet to make an impact on the unemployment rate.
Official data for January showed employment rose 38,400, almost four times the median forecast of a 10,000 rise and more than double the most optimistic forecast of a 17,000 rise.
Yet, despite the strength in employment, the unemployment rate remained unchanged at 8.6 percent due to a jump in the number of people looking for work.

"The very sharp rise in employment in January supports Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane's view that the economy is strengthening into 1997 -- and lessens the probability of a fourth rate cut," Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards said.
The stalling of the labour market was a key factor behind the three interest rates cut the Reserve Bank of Australia made between July and December last year.
On Tuesday night Macfarlane said there were signs the economy was starting to benefit from those cuts, specifically nominating investment and housing.
"And of course in employment, where the growth in employment in the last two quarters of last year was a bit higher than what they were a bit earlier in the year," Macfarlane said.
Employment has now risen by 92,900 in the last four months.

Adding to the feeling that the labour market was beginning to strengthen was the Australian Bureau of Statistics concession that a new telephone survey method had been understating monthly growth by between 6,000 to 9,000 a month since August -- meaning
that under the old survey method, the January employment level would be between 36,000 and 54,000 higher.
Even excluding that underestimation, employment has only fallen once in the last 10 months, over which time total employment has risen 158,900.
However, the number of people in the labour force has risen by 179,600 over the same 10 month period leaving the unemployment rate trapped around 8.5 percent.
Analysts said that if the growth continued, the unemployment rate should start to show signs of falling, and the still high January level was not yet a cause for renewed concern or another rate cut.

"It could well be that the unemployment rate is starting to top off and if I was a central banker looking at these numbers I would basically make sure that everything was on hold for quite a while," National Australia Bank chief economist Alan Oster said.

Some felt that the fact that the rise in employment was made up mainly of part-time jobs meant that the strength of the headline figure was overstated. However, others said that the figure should not be discounted on that basis, as part-time employment often led total employment.
"It probably tells you employers at this stage are still relatively cautious in terms of putting people on," AMP Investments chief economist Shane Oliver said.
"That's traditionally the case in the early stages of an upturn in the labour market," he said.
The recent growth in employment should also help confidence, and see consumers return to the shops after the retail sector experienced a very depressed period into the end of 1996.
"Money in people's hip pockets, irrespective of whether it's part-time or full-time, is still money in hip pockets," GIO Australia chief economist Akis Haralabopoulos said.
